section_summary: The section opens with a July 1948 despatch and enclosures assessing the Ashida cabinet, divisions within the Social Democratic Party, and the prospect of a general election. It then turns to Ichiro Hatoyama’s previously unfiled 1947 appeal against his removal from public office. The appeal, supporting remarks, and appendices argue that his record has been misread, especially his roles in the Peace Preservation Law amendment, the dismissal of a Kyoto University professor, and wartime politics.

subfiles.title: Comments of Japanese Leaders Upon the Current Political Situation
subfiles.from: H. J. Sebald, U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese leaders’ expectations of cabinet instability, party realignments, and a possible general election.
subfiles.summary: Sebald forwards two conversations and a newspaper editorial. He discusses Nishio’s resignation, Socialist divisions, efforts to form a center party, and the growing strength of Yoshida’s Democratic Liberal Party.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Tetsu Katayama on the Current Political Situation
subfiles.about: Records Katayama’s views on Nishio’s resignation, Socialist Party discipline, labor demands, and Diet dissolution.
subfiles.summary: Katayama expects Nishio to be cleared and favors firm action against the party’s extreme left wing. He foresees a difficult autumn budget session and increasingly favors an election if the coalition reaches an impasse.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Takizō Matsumoto on the Current Political Situation
subfiles.about: Records Matsumoto’s account of proposed party mergers and expectations for the Ashida cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Matsumoto describes Ashida’s interest in a merger or new center party, predicts an autumn crisis and possible election, and discusses Nishio’s and Narahashi’s political prospects.

subfiles.title: Whither the Socialist Party?
subfiles.about: Assesses whether the Socialist Party can recover from conflict over Nishio and its left wing.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that factional losses may bring unity, while greater left-wing influence could change the party’s place in government.

subfiles.title: Application of Hatoyama Ichiro Regarding Purge
subfiles.from: H. J. Sebald, U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Hatoyama’s unused 1947 application for reconsideration of his exclusion from public office.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu brought the application to the mission and said Yoshida had advised Hatoyama against filing it.

subfiles.title: Hatoyama Application: Title Page and Contents
subfiles.doc_type: title page and table of contents
subfiles.about: Identifies Hatoyama’s application, plea, evidentiary remarks, and listed appendices.
subfiles.summary: Front matter lists the appeal and its supporting articles, memoranda, cabinet records, and election materials.

subfiles.title: Application for Reconsideration of Hatoyama’s Purge
subfiles.about: Requests re-examination of SCAP’s decision barring Hatoyama from public office.
subfiles.summary: Hatoyama denies responsibility for the 1928 Peace Preservation Law amendment, disputed teacher dismissals, and suppression of legitimate labor groups. He argues that his writings and wartime conduct show opposition to militarism and support for parliamentary government.

subfiles.title: Charges and Explanations
subfiles.about: Answers the allegations underlying Hatoyama’s exclusion from public office.
subfiles.summary: Hatoyama argues that, as chief cabinet secretary, he did not formulate the Peace Preservation Law amendment and that the dismissal of Kyoto professor Takigawa was justified under the law and conditions of the time. He contests charges concerning labor suppression, his European trip, writings, and 1942 election address. He presents his wartime activity as parliamentary and anti-militarist, disputes identification with an expansionist ‘Tanaka Policy,’ and asks for a fair review of the purge decision.

subfiles.title: Evidences and Remarks
subfiles.about: Introduces and interprets the records and published statements offered in support of Hatoyama’s appeal.
subfiles.summary: Hatoyama describes cabinet papers, records on Zhang Zuolin’s assassination, a Japanese government draft explanation, writings, testimonials, and his 1942 election address. He argues that these materials establish his liberalism and opposition to militarism, and rebuts hostile accounts in the Communist newspaper Akahata.

subfiles.title: Appendix A: Cabinet Paper of June 1928
subfiles.about: Reproduces approval papers for an urgent imperial edict amending the Peace Preservation Law.
subfiles.summary: The cabinet form and recommendation concern the edict; Hatoyama points to the absence of his seal.

subfiles.title: Appendix B: Tanaka Cabinet and Assassination of General Chang Tso-lin
subfiles.doc_type: appendix; historical account with cabinet record excerpts
subfiles.about: Argues that the Tanaka cabinet did not authorize Zhang Zuolin’s assassination.
subfiles.summary: The appendix quotes investigations, reports, and Tanaka’s communications about the 1928 train bombing near Mukden. It says a small group of Kwantung Army officers acted without cabinet knowledge, that Tanaka later learned the truth, and that the cabinet resigned after his false initial report to the emperor. Hatoyama uses this account to dispute the portrayal of a unified expansionist ‘Tanaka Policy.’

subfiles.title: Appendix C: Draft Japanese Government Explanation Concerning Hatoyama
subfiles.about: Presents an unsubmitted draft assessment of Hatoyama’s book and the dismissal of Professor Takigawa.
subfiles.summary: The draft argues that Hatoyama’s travel book does not establish support for Nazism, fascism, or militarism. It describes the 1933 Kyoto Imperial University dismissal of Takigawa and asks that Hatoyama’s responsibility be judged in the circumstances of the time. The appendix continues beyond page 67.
